Yardney Electric Corporation, USA, designs, develops and manufactures Silver Zinc, Nickel Cadmium and Silver Chloride Magnesium batteries for high-rate, mission-critical applications such as aviation starting/emergency power, torpedo propulsion, satellite launch vehicles and army battle tanks. risks.risk: Concentration in Defence sector demand, tied to Government budget cycles
risks.note: The Company's major revenue is from the Defence sector and is dependent on Defence priorities and budget allocation; demand is not regular in nature as the ordering schedule is cyclic and volumes are not large since the application is strategic Defence use, more as a deterrent.

risks.risk: Lengthening and unpredictable Defence order-placement cycle
risks.note: The procurement cycle has shifted from four-to-five years historically to six-to-seven years or more, and a change in Government procurement policy (especially by Defence Departments) is explicitly flagged as a threat that could affect order timing and revenue visibility.

risks.risk: Customer concentration within the Aerospace & Naval segment
risks.note: HEB derives around 60% of Aerospace and Naval segment revenue from Navy & Naval Research Labs, with Navy & Naval Research Labs also accounting for ~58% of the overall customer order mix.

risks.risk: Raw material price volatility (Silver, Zinc, Copper)
risks.note: Major raw materials are Silver, Zinc and Copper, whose prices are highly volatile due to external market factors; an abrupt increase in raw material prices could compress margins, though silver price volatility is largely covered via a price variation clause built into customer contracts.
The Company has a long working capital cycle, primarily due to the higher levels of inventory that need to be maintained for its Defence-oriented, cyclic-order business.

risks.risk: Import and Forex exposure on critical materials/components
risks.note: Less than 10% of total raw materials consumed are imported, but these are liable to Forex variation and/or Government import restrictions and delays; the AR also separately flags import restriction/delay in receipt of critical materials/components as a threat.

risks.risk: Regulatory constraints on exports and strategic-secrecy obligations
risks.note: The Company requires prior permission from the Ministry of Defence to export, and its principal-customer relationships with Defence Supplies and VSSC/ISRO subject it to provisions of the Official Secrets Act, 1923, limiting disclosure and export flexibility even though export markets are being explored (Poland, Vietnam, Philippines, Malaysia, Algeria, Italy, Kyrgyzstan).

Management flags the introduction of advanced and/or disruptive systems and technological breakthroughs as a threat, along with the necessity to get trained in upcoming technologies and upgrade production methods and equipment to remain competitive.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: High Energy Batteries (India) Limited, established in 1979 with technical collaboration from M/s. Yardney Electric Corporation, USA, designs, develops and manufactures Silver Zinc, Nickel Cadmium and Silver Chloride Magnesium batteries for high-rate, mission-critical applications such as aviation starting/emergency power, torpedo propulsion, satellite launch vehicles and army battle tanks. Its principal customers are the Department of Defence Supplies and VSSC/ISRO. The Company also has a Lead Acid Battery division (operations suspended since April 2019) and is developing Fuel Cells and Vanadium Redox Flow Batteries (VRFB) for Energy Storage Systems (ESS) applications.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Revenue grew at a CAGR of 6% over the last ten years (FY2016-17 to FY2025-26), backed by Government's thrust on the Defence sector and its focus on awarding orders to indigenous players
- Defence procurement order-placement cycle has lengthened from four-to-five years historically to six-to-seven years or more, reflecting mid-life technical improvements (via in-house R&D) that extend both dry and wet storage life of batteries in service
- Competitive pricing requirements in recent years are impacting operating margins, versus greater pricing flexibility in earlier years
- EBITDA margins have improved substantially over the last five years due to a change in product mix, better absorption of fixed costs and improved banking operations
- India's Energy Storage System (ESS) market is transitioning from a nascent pilot phase to core grid infrastructure to support the country's 500 GW renewable energy target, with the BESS market projected to grow from USD 2.05 billion in 2026 to USD 8.59 billion by 2031 at a 33.2% CAGR, driven by renewable energy integration, EV adoption, government mandates (Energy Storage Obligations) and declining costs via Viability Gap Funding
- Central Electricity Authority estimates India will require 411.4 GWh of energy storage (split between BESS and Pumped Hydro Storage) by 2031-32, with the BESS project pipeline already at 92 GWh
- Union Budget FY2026-27 raised Ministry of Defence's total budget by 15.19% YoY to Rs 7.85 lakh crore, with Rs 1.39 lakh crore earmarked for domestic Defence industry procurement and capital acquisition allocation up ~24% YoY to Rs 1.85 lakh crore, supporting demand visibility for indigenous defence suppliers
- Indian Defence exports rose 62.66% YoY to Rs 38,424 crore in FY2025-26, indicating a growing export opportunity for domestic Defence manufacturers
- Confirmed order book of around Rs 56 Crores with a possible order value of Rs 101 Crores to be realized within the next 6 months and executed over the next 12-18 months, compared to the previous year's opening order book of Rs 62.68 Crores, providing revenue visibility for FY2026-27
- Typical customer order mix: Navy & Naval Research Labs ~58%, Defence Public Sector ~15%, Aerospace & Others (NICAD, TDF and NuPro) ~27%; Aerospace and Naval segment derives around 60% of revenue from Navy & Naval Research Labs

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Expand product range to include Fuel Cells (for power generation using Hydrogen) and Flow Battery, mainly Vanadium Redox Flow Battery/VRFB (for bulk energy storage / LDES applications)
- Focus more on value-added products including Lithium Ion based Battery/Power Pack System Integration to occupy a strong position in both Defence-related and non-Defence markets in India
- Pursue Engineering and Development work on multi-kW level BESS (Battery Energy Storage System) programs to participate in India's grid-scale storage build-out
- Continue to explore export potential for products on a continuous basis, though limited by Ministry of Defence export-permission requirements
- Leverage Government's continued thrust on indigenization and Atmanirbhar in Defence procurement, which favours domestic manufacturers with in-house Design, Development and manufacturing-cum-testing capability
- For FY2025-26 a dividend of Rs 3 per equity share (face value Rs 2 each) was recommended/declared to shareholders as on the record date, subject to shareholder approval at the 65th AGM. Separately, shareholder approval was sought (Special Business at the AGM) to pay commission to Non-Executive Directors out of net profit, exclusive of sitting fees, for three financial years from FY2026-27 to FY2028-29, capped within Section 197 of the Companies Act, 2013 limits.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The Company already operates a dedicated Production-cum-Testing facility for manufacture of High-Power Batteries for Strategic Defence Applications. Beyond its existing Silver Zinc, Nickel Cadmium and Silver Chloride Magnesium battery lines, HEB is working to expand its product range into Fuel Cells (for Hydrogen-based power generation) and Flow Battery, mainly Vanadium Redox Flow Battery (VRFB), for bulk/long-duration energy storage (LDES) applications, and is pursuing Engineering and Development work on multi-kW level Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) programs to participate in India's grid-scale storage build-out (CEA estimates India will need 411.4 GWh of energy storage by 2031-32, split between BESS and Pumped Hydro Storage).
